question: At the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, professional NBA players were allowed to compete for the first time, assembling a roster of legends like Michael Jordan, Magic Johnson, and Larry Bird that dominated every opponent by an average of over 40 points. Which country did this legendary 'Dream Team' represent?

options.info: Won gold at Barcelona 1992 by an average margin of over 40 points per game.
Faced the Dream Team in the 1992 gold medal game and took silver.
Also competed in 1992, famously wearing tie-dye jerseys sponsored by the Grateful Dead.
Hosted the 1992 Games but didn't reach the gold medal game.

question: The Olympic marathon's odd distance of 26 miles and 385 yards wasn't set by the ancient Greek legend it's named after, but by a specific modern Olympic Games that extended the course to finish in front of a royal viewing box. Which Games fixed this now-standard distance?

options.info: The course was extended so the race could finish in front of the royal box at White City Stadium.
The first modern marathon, run at roughly 40 km, not the standardized modern distance.
Adopted the 1908 distance as the permanent standard, but didn't create it.
Notable for Jesse Owens' four gold medals, not the marathon distance.

question: Between 2004 and 2016, one American swimmer won 23 Olympic gold medals, more than most entire countries have ever won across all sports combined. Who is he?

options.info: Won 23 Olympic golds across five Games, the most of any Olympian ever.
Held the record for golds in a single Games (7, in 1972) before Phelps surpassed it.
A teammate and rival of Phelps's, but far behind his total medal count.
Australian swimmer nicknamed 'Thorpedo,' with 5 Olympic golds.

question: In 1974, a heavyweight title fight nicknamed the 'Rumble in the Jungle' was held in Kinshasa, Zaire (today's Democratic Republic of Congo), where the underdog challenger used his famous 'rope-a-dope' tactic to reclaim the world title. Who was that challenger?

options.info: Defeated George Foreman by knockout in the eighth round to reclaim the heavyweight title.
The reigning champion Ali defeated that night.
Ali's great rival, but not the challenger in the Rumble in the Jungle.
An earlier Ali opponent from the 1960s, not part of this fight.

question: Before international rugby matches, one national team performs a traditional Māori challenge with rhythmic chanting, foot-stamping, and fierce facial expressions, intended to intimidate opponents before kickoff. Which country's team is famous for this haka?

options.info: The All Blacks perform the haka, most famously the version called 'Ka Mate.'
A fierce rugby rival of New Zealand's, but doesn't perform the haka.
Performs its own pre-match challenge, called the cibi, not the haka.
Performs the siva tau, a different traditional pre-match challenge.

question: Though it's now most passionately followed in South Asia and cricket-mad island nations, this bat-and-ball sport's earliest recorded matches were played by shepherds and farmers in medieval fields. In which country did cricket originate?

options.info: Cricket's earliest recorded matches date to 16th-century southern England.
Now cricket's most passionate fanbase and biggest market, but not its birthplace.
A cricket powerhouse and home to the historic Ashes rivalry, but not its birthplace.
A dominant cricket force for decades, but not where the sport began.

question: In 1977, a low-budget space opera about a farm boy, a princess, and a smuggler became a cultural phenomenon and launched one of the biggest franchises in film history. Who created and directed the original Star Wars?

options.info: Wrote and directed the original 1977 Star Wars film.
A close friend and collaborator of Lucas's, but didn't direct Star Wars.
Directed Alien around the same era, a different sci-fi franchise.
Later directed Titanic and Avatar, not Star Wars.

question: Centered in Mumbai and known for song-and-dance numbers woven into nearly every genre, this film industry produces more movies per year than any other in the world. What is it commonly nicknamed?

options.info: India's Hindi-language film industry, based in Mumbai (formerly Bombay).
Nigeria's prolific film industry, the world's second-largest by output.
Pakistan's film industry, based in Lahore.
Refers to India's Telugu- or Bengali-language film industries.

question: In 2020, a dark comedy-thriller about class divide became the first non-English-language film ever to win the Academy Award for Best Picture. Which South Korean director made it?

options.info: Directed Parasite, which swept four Oscars including Best Picture.
Known for Oldboy, another acclaimed South Korean director.
South Korean director known for spare, meditative films.
Acclaimed South Korean director of Burning and Poetry.

question: A chemistry teacher turned methamphetamine kingpin was the subject of a critically acclaimed drama that ran from 2008 to 2013 and later spawned the spinoff 'Better Call Saul.' Which US cable network originally aired 'Breaking Bad'?

options.info: Aired Breaking Bad from 2008 to 2013, and Better Call Saul afterward.
Home to prestige dramas like The Sopranos, but not Breaking Bad.
Known for shows like It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia, not Breaking Bad.
Known for dramas like Dexter and Homeland, not Breaking Bad.

question: For over a decade, one 1997 film about a doomed ocean liner held the record for highest-grossing movie of all time, until the same director's own 'Avatar' eventually topped it. Who directed 'Titanic'?

options.info: Directed both Titanic (1997) and Avatar (2009), each a box-office record holder.
Directed other blockbusters like Jaws and Jurassic Park, not Titanic.
Directed Apollo 13, another 1990s disaster-adjacent film, not Titanic.
Known for big-budget action films, but didn't direct Titanic.

question: Known for hand-drawn animation, environmental themes, and films like 'Spirited Away' and 'My Neighbor Totoro,' this Japanese studio was co-founded by a director often called the 'Japanese Walt Disney.' Who is he?

options.info: Co-founded Studio Ghibli and directed most of its best-known films.
Legendary Japanese live-action director of Seven Samurai, not an animator.
Acclaimed Japanese anime director known for Perfect Blue and Paprika.
Ghibli's co-founder, directed Grave of the Fireflies, but not these particular films.

question: Commissioned for a Moscow theater and now a holiday season staple worldwide, a ballet about a magical nutcracker toy that comes to life on Christmas Eve premiered in 1892. Which Russian composer wrote it, along with 'Swan Lake'?

options.info: Composed both The Nutcracker and Swan Lake.
Composed The Rite of Spring and The Firebird, a generation later.
Composed Romeo and Juliet and Peter and the Wolf, not the Nutcracker.
20th-century Soviet composer known for symphonies, not this ballet.

question: Nicknamed 'The Red Priest' for his flame-colored hair and clerical training, this Baroque composer wrote a set of four violin concertos that musically depict spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Who was he?

options.info: Composed The Four Seasons, one of the most recorded works in classical music.
A contemporary Baroque composer, but not the writer of The Four Seasons.
An earlier Italian Baroque composer known for concerti grossi.
Italian Baroque composer famous for harpsichord sonatas.

question: A child prodigy who was composing and touring European royal courts by age six, this Austrian composer left behind an unfinished Requiem Mass at his death in 1791. Who was he?

options.info: Died before finishing his Requiem, which was later completed by a student.
Mozart's older friend and mentor, sometimes called the 'Father of the Symphony.'
A court composer and Mozart's rumored rival, though the rivalry is largely legend.
An earlier opera reformer, not the composer of this unfinished Requiem.

question: Opening in 1778 after a fire destroyed Milan's previous royal theater, this opera house has hosted the premieres of works by Verdi and Puccini and remains one of the most prestigious opera venues in the world. What's it called?

options.info: Milan's legendary opera house, opened in 1778.
Another world-famous opera house, but located in Austria, not Milan.
London's leading opera venue, in Covent Garden.
Moscow's historic opera and ballet theatre, not in Italy.

question: Lying on his back atop scaffolding for roughly four years, this Renaissance artist painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, including the iconic scene of God reaching out to touch Adam's finger. Who was he?

options.info: Painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling between 1508 and 1512.
Painted The School of Athens in a nearby Vatican room, not the ceiling.
Painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, not the Sistine ceiling.
An earlier Renaissance sculptor, best known for his bronze David.

question: Known for unflinching self-portraits exploring pain, identity, and Mexican culture, often featuring her own unibrow and vivid symbolism, this 20th-century painter was married to muralist Diego Rivera. Who was she?

options.info: Painted dozens of self-portraits exploring physical and emotional pain.
Kahlo's husband, himself famous for large political murals rather than self-portraits.
A Spanish-Mexican surrealist painter, a contemporary of Kahlo's.
A Brazilian modernist painter, not married to Rivera.

question: During a five-year voyage aboard HMS Beagle, this British naturalist studied finches and tortoises on the Galápagos Islands, observations that later fed into his theory of evolution by natural selection. Who was he?

options.info: Published On the Origin of Species in 1859, decades after his Beagle voyage.
Independently developed a similar theory of natural selection around the same time.
Austrian monk whose pea-plant experiments founded modern genetics.
Nicknamed 'Darwin's Bulldog' for fiercely defending his theory publicly.

question: In 1928, a Scottish scientist returned from vacation to find mold had contaminated one of his bacteria cultures — and noticed the mold seemed to be killing the bacteria around it. That accidental discovery led to the first antibiotic. Who made it?

options.info: His discovery of penicillin later earned him a Nobel Prize.
Pioneered germ theory and pasteurization decades earlier, not penicillin.
Identified the bacteria behind tuberculosis and cholera, not penicillin.
Developed the polio vaccine in the 1950s, unrelated to antibiotics.

question: Long thought to be effectively instantaneous, light actually travels at a specific, finite speed that Einstein's theory of relativity treats as an unbreakable cosmic speed limit. Roughly how fast does light travel in a vacuum?

options.info: The precise value is 299,792,458 meters per second.
Far too slow — that's roughly the speed of a fast jet, not light.
About 100 times too slow to be light's actual speed.
About 10 times too slow to be light's actual speed.

question: Inside chloroplasts, plants capture sunlight and use it to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen, a process essential to almost all life on Earth. What is this process called?

options.info: Converts light energy into chemical energy stored as glucose.
The process cells use to release energy from glucose, roughly the reverse.
A different energy-releasing process used by yeast and some bacteria.
The evaporation of water from plant leaves, a separate process.

question: According to popular legend, this English scientist first conceived of universal gravitation after watching an apple fall from a tree in his family's garden, later formalizing the laws of motion in his 1687 work 'Principia Mathematica.' Who was he?

options.info: Formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation.
Studied falling objects and motion decades earlier, but didn't formulate universal gravitation.
Described planetary orbits mathematically, without explaining the underlying force.
A rival scientist who also worked on gravity, and clashed with Newton over credit.

question: Each typical human cell nucleus contains DNA packaged into a specific number of chromosomes, arranged in 23 pairs, one set inherited from each parent. How many chromosomes does that add up to?

options.info: 23 pairs, one inherited from each parent.
That's the number of pairs, not the total chromosome count.
Close, but two short of the actual human total.
That's the chromosome count for chimpanzees, our closest living relatives.

question: Built in the 12th century as a Hindu temple and later converted for Buddhist worship, this vast complex sprawling across the jungle is considered the largest religious monument in the world. In which country is it located?

options.info: Angkor Wat was built by the Khmer Empire near Siem Reap.
Home to Borobudur, another huge ancient temple, but not Angkor Wat.
Home to thousands of ancient temples at Bagan, but not Angkor Wat.
Shares regional Buddhist temple traditions, but not this particular monument.

question: In 1324, a West African ruler set out on a pilgrimage to Mecca with a caravan so enormous and laden with gold that his spending reportedly disrupted the economies of the cities he passed through, including Cairo. Which empire did he rule?

options.info: Ruled by Mansa Musa, often cited as history's wealthiest individual.
A later West African empire that eventually eclipsed Mali.
A West African kingdom based further south, in what's now Ghana.
An East African empire, unrelated to this famous pilgrimage.

question: By volume of water discharged, this South American river dwarfs every other river on Earth, carrying more water than the next several largest rivers combined. Which river is it?

options.info: Discharges more water than the next several largest rivers combined.
Often cited as the longest river by length, but carries far less water.
North America's largest river system, but a fraction of the Amazon's discharge.
Asia's longest river, but well behind the Amazon in volume.

question: Built on an island in a lake and connected to the mainland by causeways, this Aztec capital amazed Spanish conquistadors with its scale before it was destroyed and rebuilt as the foundation of today's Mexico City. What was it called?

options.info: The Aztec capital, conquered by Hernán Cortés in 1521.
The Inca capital, located in the Andes of Peru, not the Aztec Empire.
An earlier, mysterious Mesoamerican city, already abandoned by Aztec times.
A major Maya city in the Yucatán, not the Aztec capital.

question: Some estimates put the arrival of the first humans in this continent at over 65,000 years ago, making its Indigenous peoples' culture among the oldest continuous living cultures on Earth. Which continent?

options.info: Aboriginal Australians' culture is often cited as the oldest continuous living culture.
Humans arrived there much later, tens of thousands of years after Australia.
Also settled later than Australia, via land bridges from Asia.
Has no Indigenous population at all — it was never permanently inhabited.

question: Completed in 1914 after a failed earlier French attempt, this artificial waterway cuts through a narrow strip of land to let ships pass between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans without sailing around South America. What's it called?

options.info: Completed by the United States in 1914 after France's earlier attempt failed.
Connects the Mediterranean and Red Seas, in Egypt, not the Americas.
A much smaller canal cutting through mainland Greece.
Connects the North Sea and Baltic Sea, through northern Germany.

question: Rising dramatically from surrounding savanna to over 5,800 meters, its snow-capped peak visible for miles despite sitting just south of the equator, this is Africa's tallest mountain. In which country is it located?

options.info: Mount Kilimanjaro is Africa's highest peak, at about 5,895 meters.
Home to its own notable peak, Mount Kenya, but not Kilimanjaro.
Home to the Rwenzori Mountains, not Kilimanjaro.
Has high mountainous terrain, but not Africa's tallest peak.

question: In the early 1200s, one leader united the nomadic tribes of the Mongolian steppe and launched a series of conquests that would create the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Eastern Europe. Who was he?

options.info: Founded the Mongol Empire, the largest contiguous land empire in history.
Genghis Khan's grandson, who later founded China's Yuan Dynasty.
A later Central Asian conqueror, active in the 14th century.
Led an earlier, separate nomadic empire centuries before the Mongols.

question: In 1868, after centuries of relative isolation under shogun rule, this East Asian country began a rapid, top-down transformation into an industrialized, modern military and economic power. What is this transformation commonly called?

options.info: Restored imperial rule in Japan and launched rapid industrialization.
A very different, later political upheaval in Communist China.
A massive 19th-century Chinese civil war, unrelated to Japan's reforms.
The 1911 revolution that ended China's imperial dynasty system.

question: At just over 0.4 square kilometers, this independent city-state entirely surrounded by Rome is the smallest country in the world by both area and population. What is it called?

options.info: The world's smallest sovereign state, home to the Pope.
Another tiny European microstate, but larger than the Vatican and not inside Rome.
A small, densely populated country on the French Riviera, not in Italy.
A small Alpine country between Austria and Switzerland, not in Italy.

question: Founded around 930 AD by early Norse settlers who gathered annually at a site called Þingvellir to settle disputes and make laws, this assembly is often cited as the world's oldest still-functioning parliament. Which country's parliament is it?

options.info: The Althing has met, in some form, since around 930 AD.
The homeland of many of Iceland's original settlers, but not where this assembly meets.
Ruled Iceland for centuries later, but didn't found this ancient assembly.
Also has an old Norse-founded assembly, but a younger and smaller one.

question: Perched on a limestone rock at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula, this small territory has been under British control since 1713, despite Spain's continuing claims to it. What's it called?

options.info: A British Overseas Territory since the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713.
A Spanish-controlled enclave on the North African coast, not British.
An independent microstate in the Pyrenees, not a British territory.
A Spanish Balearic island, once British-controlled but not today.

question: Roughly a quarter of this country's land lies below sea level, protected by an extensive system of dikes, dams, and pumps, with large areas of reclaimed "polder" farmland won directly from the sea over centuries. Which country is it?

options.info: About a quarter of its land lies below sea level.
Shares a coastline and some low-lying terrain, but far less below sea level.
Low and flat, but doesn't rely on this scale of land reclamation from the sea.
Has North Sea coastline, but nowhere near this proportion below sea level.

question: Invented in 1974 by a Hungarian architecture professor as a teaching tool to help explain three-dimensional geometry, this twisty puzzle cube became one of the best-selling toys of all time. Who invented it?

options.info: Originally called it the 'Magic Cube' before it was renamed after him.
Created a different iconic puzzle: the video game Tetris.
A mathematician known for the Game of Life, not the Rubik's Cube.
An American board game manufacturer, not the cube's inventor.

question: Blinded in a childhood accident, this 19th-century Frenchman developed a system of raised dots that could be read by touch, now used worldwide to let blind and visually impaired people read and write. What's his name, now used for the system itself?

options.info: Developed the tactile reading system as a teenager in the 1820s.
French author of The Little Prince, unrelated to this writing system.
French novelist known for Les Misérables, not the braille system.
The French diplomat nicotine is named after, unrelated to braille.

question: By European Union law, only sparkling wine produced in a specific northeastern French region, using specific grape varieties and methods, is legally allowed to carry this name — everything else must be called sparkling wine or something else entirely. What is this protected name?

options.info: Legally restricted to sparkling wine from the Champagne region of France.
Italian sparkling wine, made differently and from different grapes.
Spanish sparkling wine, made in the traditional method but not from Champagne.
French sparkling wine made outside the Champagne region.

question: Designed in the 1870s for early mechanical typewriters, this keyboard letter layout was arranged partly to keep commonly paired letters physically apart, reducing jams in the machine's typebars. What is this layout commonly called, after its top-left letter row?

options.info: Named for the first six letters on the top row.
A French variant of the keyboard layout, with some letters swapped.
A German-language variant layout, with Y and Z swapped.
A later keyboard layout designed for typing efficiency, not to prevent jams.

question: A researcher at this American company was trying to develop a super-strong adhesive in 1968 but accidentally created a very weak, reusable one instead — an invention that sat unused for years until a colleague used it to bookmark his hymn book, leading to one of the best-selling office products ever. Which company was it?

options.info: The accidental adhesive became the basis for Post-it Notes, launched in 1980.
American chemical company known for inventing nylon and Teflon.
A major US consumer goods company, unrelated to Post-it Notes.
An American industrial conglomerate, not the inventor of Post-it Notes.

question: Invented in 1886 by an Atlanta pharmacist as a patent medicine and originally sold at soda fountains, this drink's exact flavor recipe remains one of the most famous trade secrets in business history. What's the drink?

options.info: Created by pharmacist John Pemberton in Atlanta, Georgia.
Invented a few years later, in 1893, by a different pharmacist in North Carolina.
Invented around the same era in Waco, Texas, by a different pharmacist.
A broader category of drink with roots in earlier folk recipes, not a single 1886 invention.

question: Its 1875 Paris premiere was treated as a scandal: the heroine smokes, brawls, refuses to belong to anyone, and is stabbed to death on stage — in a theatre whose audiences came expecting respectable family entertainment. The composer died of a heart attack three months later at 36, convinced he had written a flop. Within a decade it was among the most performed operas in the world. Who wrote it?

options.info: 'Carmen' is now a repertory staple everywhere; he never saw it succeed.
A French contemporary whose 'Manon' and 'Werther' arrived later and had far smoother premieres.
His 'Faust' was the great French operatic hit of the previous generation; he was in fact Bizet's mentor.
The king of Parisian operetta, remembered for the can-can from 'Orpheus in the Underworld'.

question: Audiences in the 1820s half-believed this Italian violinist had struck a bargain with the devil: he played passages other violinists thought physically impossible, kept going on the remaining strings when others snapped mid-performance, and refused to publish most of his caprices so nobody could steal his techniques. Who was he?

options.info: A likely connective-tissue disorder may explain his freakish finger reach. The church initially refused him a burial in consecrated ground.
An earlier Italian violinist who really did claim a dream of the devil playing — the source of his 'Devil's Trill' sonata.
A Baroque violinist and composer whose elegant sonatas set the standard a century before this.
Not a performer at all — the Cremonese luthier whose instruments the great violinists competed to own.

question: Around 1700 the keeper of instruments at the Medici court in Florence solved a frustration that had nagged keyboard players for generations: a harpsichord plucks its strings, so pressing harder changes nothing. His mechanism struck the strings with leather-covered hammers that immediately fell away, and the result was catalogued as a harpsichord that could play soft and loud. Which craftsman is credited with that invention?

options.info: Three of his instruments survive. The full original name of his invention, 'gravicembalo col piano e forte', is where the modern short name comes from.
A German builder who improved on the design decades later and sold the results to Frederick the Great.
Augsburg builder of the light-actioned Viennese instruments that Mozart's generation preferred.
The Parisian firm behind the double-escapement action of 1821, which allowed fast repeated notes on the modern grand.

question: Formed in Düsseldorf in 1970, this group performed motionless in matching suits behind four identical consoles, and later commissioned lifelike mannequins of themselves to appear at photo calls and even parts of concerts in their place. Their rigid electronic records went on to underpin hip hop, techno and synth-pop alike. Which band?

options.info: Afrika Bambaataa's 'Planet Rock' famously built on two of their tracks, and Detroit techno producers cited them constantly.
A Cologne group from the same era, but improvisational and rhythm-section-driven rather than machine-precise.
Berlin pioneers of long-form electronic soundscapes and film scores, with no robot-persona concept.
A duo formed by two ex-members of this very scene, remembered for the relentless 'motorik' drumbeat.

question: At the 1976 Montreal Olympics the scoreboard software had been built on the assumption that a certain result was impossible, so it could only show three digits. When a 14-year-old gymnast produced the first flawless routine in Olympic history, her mark flashed up as 1.00 and the crowd needed a moment to work out what had happened. Who was she?

options.info: The Romanian went on to score seven perfect tens at those Games and left Montreal with three golds.
The Soviet gymnast whose charm at the 1972 Munich Games created the audience that watched Montreal.
Czechoslovak great of the 1960s, remembered for quietly turning her head away during a medal ceremony in 1968.
A Soviet all-around champion of the same era, admired for precision but never awarded a perfect ten.

question: A Senegalese dockworker turned novelist concluded in the 1960s that books were reaching only the small literate minority at home, so he taught himself to make films instead. His 1966 feature about a young woman taken to the French Riviera to work as a maid is usually called the first film by a sub-Saharan African director to reach international audiences. Who was he?

options.info: Often called the father of African cinema; he later switched to shooting in Wolof rather than French so audiences at home could follow without subtitles.
Another Senegalese director, whose surreal 1973 road film 'Touki Bouki' came later and took a very different approach.
The Malian director of 'Yeelen', which won at Cannes in 1987.
Mauritanian director and voice actor whose militant 'Soleil Ô' appeared in 1970.

question: In 1967 a graduate student in Cambridge was working through hundreds of metres of chart paper from a radio telescope she had helped build when she noticed a smear of signal that turned out to be pulsing every 1.3 seconds — so regular the team half-jokingly labelled the source LGM-1, for 'Little Green Men'. It was in fact a rapidly spinning neutron star. The Nobel Prize for the discovery went to her supervisor. Who spotted it?

options.info: She was left off the 1974 physics Nobel; in 2018 she won a $3 million Breakthrough Prize and immediately gave the money away as scholarships.
An earlier British-American astronomer who showed that stars are made mostly of hydrogen.
The American astronomer whose galaxy rotation measurements pointed to dark matter — also famously passed over for a Nobel.
Classified several hundred thousand stellar spectra at Harvard, creating the system still used today.
